chapters.s: To all who had stayed awake through the night, morning came that day not late but suddenly. Channa Grove, which for centuries had seemed to hold dawn back, now, as a half-cut stump, let the sun enter without a curtain for the first time. The yellow paper was pasted onto the stump. The children stopped playing. Budhba Ghost thickened again in the gathering darkness. Panidubbi smiled beneath the water—the market had arrived.…

For the first time people sat in a round circle around the stump. Earlier, when entering Channa Grove, people bowed their heads, and it was hard to know whether this was because the branches hung low or the darkness pressed down. Thus the first day around the stump did not really end. It sat waiting for the next hearing. The tree had been cut, but around it a circle of people had grown. And at the centre of that circle the yellow envelope, like a dry leaf…

All night the yellow envelope lay upon the rim of the stump. One by one the lamps went out and people's voices withdrew, yet a corner of the envelope kept fluttering in the wind. The yellow notice remained upon the rim of the stump. Its seal was dimming, but the people's written word “Present” shone. On the first night facing the seven-day threat, Garh Narikel sat down to draw its first map of memory.

All night the words of the yellow notice fluttered upon the rim of the stump. The phrase “empty plot” entered everyone's sleep like a thorn. Night descended. The map hung behind the stump—river, tree, hole, palm, circle of privacy, the imagined question of the “Unnamed Planet.” And the proposal, polite from the outside, perhaps hid within it the first tooth of the most cunning crocodile yet.

For one night between the yellow notice and the first map of memory, the stump of Channa Grove was so restless that its severed roots seemed to turn from within. The children's map lay spread on the soil—the Kamala-Balan, the bridge piers, the feet of water-burial, Ujjwal's room, Mira's oath, Devika's school… Gangesha's question was not finished. After the paper trust, a screen trust was arriving. A faint laugh rose from inside the stump—as though Navya-Nyaya itself were ready to examine the proof of the next deception.

By dawn Chandrapal Batra's “Digital Tribute Platform” had begun glowing on many phones in Garh Narikel. The message said: “Make the name of your loved one immortal, preserve memory safely, offer tribute.” Beneath it were flowers, a lamp, water, and a small shining symbol. All night the children kept watch around the stump. One watched the glow of mobile phones, one the names on the stones, one the yellow notice, one the red file. Channa Grove had been cut, but four crocodiles now lay in wait around its courtyard—government…

The next morning people sat around the stump to read Raghav’s code as though an ancient scripture were about to be opened. But this scripture was written not on leaves, but on the blurred traces of a vanished screen. All night the kabaddi line glimmered faintly in the soil. The children kept watch. The name-stones remained in place. The yellow notice was silent. The red file stayed closed. The memorial app’s screen went dark.…

When Raghav “Signal” Somani’s new code reached the circle around the stump, at first no one understood its meaning. On paper everything was written in the language of piety—offering, reverence, rebuilding, memorial support, fund for victims’ families. When he rose to leave, wind passed through a split in the stump and sounded behind him: “Kabaddi.” Satyavrat stopped. The field was empty, the children had gone home, the ghosts were invisible. Yet the line had been drawn.…

The morning of the Festival of Names did not arrive like a village fair. No drums sounded, no flags flew, no chairs were arranged on a platform while speakers were awaited. The stump stayed awake through the night. The sound of the reading of names had sunk into the soil. The white trust paper and the yellow notice lay beside each other and trembled, as though both had understood that the rule of paper would not be simple here.…

chapters.t: A Green Point in the Stump
chapters.s: The night of the First Festival of Names passed, but the lamps burning around the stump of Channa Grove did not go out before dawn. Their wicks had grown small and the oil was nearly finished, yet the flames were stubborn, as though the watch over names had taken residence inside them. At night, after everyone had gone home, a sheet of paper blew toward the stump. It bore no government seal, but it was as smooth as a consultant’s draft. Across the top, in bold letters, stood: “Garh Narikel Heritage Corridor…

On the third day after the green point broke from the stump, government vehicles arrived in the village for the first time without embarrassment. Earlier, whenever Channa Grove was mentioned, officials hid their faces behind files. At dawn Ananya saw the paper. She opened the register and wrote on a blank line: “Today memory was put out to tender.” Then she looked toward the green leaf on the stump. It did not tremble. It seemed to be saying: “Now the struggle has begun.”

Not even three days had passed since the Garh Narikel Heritage Project was announced when identical white notices appeared on the tehsil wall, the municipal gate, bus-stand pillars and the half-broken bridge pier.… Ananya wrote the night’s final sentence in the register: “A tender has come for memory. The bidder is still hiding his name.” Then she closed the page. The smell of the river came from afar on the wind.…

The moment the tender for memory was opened, an old smell rose from within it. It was not the smell of paper, nor of fresh ink, nor of government dust. The green point on the stump opened a little further that night. Broom's letter fluttered in the wind as though some old crocodile from a distant seacoast had begun smelling the water again. Garh Narikel remained silent, but its silence now kept watch.…

On the third morning after Broom's return, a strange vehicle came to Garh Narikel. Its windows were black, small devices were fixed on its roof, and identity cards gleamed at the throats of the people seated inside. The filmmaker still held his camera, but dust from Channa Grove had settled on its lens. He moved to clean it, and in the dust he saw not his own face but a crocodile's eye. He lowered the camera.…

chapters.t: Meera and the Right to Sight
chapters.s: When Harvard's research team returned to the Channa stump on the second day, they did not sit down and open their notebooks as before. This time cameras hung from their necks, bright bags swung from their shoulders, and there was a strange haste in their eyes. The green point on the stump glowed faintly in the night, as though the tree were saying: the watch over sight is in place, but the market of memory is still awake.

The peace that should have descended upon Garh Narikel after the Festival of Names did not come. In the place where the children read names, where the green point on the stump squinted in sunlight, where Meera kept watch over the dignity of faces and the right to sight… Ananya opened the register. On the first page she wrote: “From today, the theft of names has begun.” Devika looked toward the stump. The green point was still there, but the soil around it appeared slightly disturbed.…

When Devika exposed the lie of the tribute app before everyone, the people thought the real theft had been caught. But the Channa stump knew that the theft caught on a screen was only the bright page of theft. The chapter paused where the theft of names began turning into the testimony of water. The next morning the people of Garh Narikel would gather by the pond, and for the first time the Panidubbi would speak in a clear voice…

Budhba's words—“Water keeps an erased name”—and Ananya's written resolve, “Tomorrow we shall listen to the pond,” throbbed in the village's heart all night. No one in Garh Narikel slept well after the night of the theft of names. Thus the Panidubbi's testimony did not end. Instead, it opened the next danger: memory saved by water was now something the market wished to turn into performance.…

The smell of fresh paste on the poster had not yet dried when preparations for the festival reached the village. On the second day after the submarine's testimony, a new vehicle arrived in Garh Narikel. Someone asked, “Did the tree laugh?” Ba replied, “Yes. When memory begins to be sold and yet survives, a tree laughs.” The children were not startled. They opened the next page. At the top they wrote: “The Laughter of Channa Grove.”

The heading written on the new page of the children's register—“The Laughter of Channa Grove”—began telling its own story by dawn. The laughter that had risen after the procession of false ghosts collapsed did not remain merely an incident of one night. And inside that circle of laughter, Batuknath's dream court opened.
